title: "Computing engines and control of VLMC with covariates"
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: 72
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(mixvlmc)
```

A VLMC with covariates (COVLMC, see `vignette("covlmc")`) associates a
logistic model to each of its contexts. Those models are fitted by
external packages, called *computing engines* in `mixvlmc`. This article
describes the available engines, their differences and the parameters
that control the estimation of the logistic models. It also explains how
to reduce the memory occupied by COVLMC objects, which store the fitted
models.

## Computing engines

### Choosing an engine

The engine is selected with the `mixvlmc.predictive` option (see
`?mixvlmc-package` for the list of the package options). Two values are
supported:

- `"glm"` (default value): `covlmc()` uses `stats::glm()` with the
  binomial family when the time series has two states, and
  `VGAM::vglm()` with the multinomial family when it has three states
  or more;
- `"multinom"`: `covlmc()` uses `nnet::multinom()` in all cases.

The engine can be changed for the rest of the session with `options()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
old_options <- options(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom")
## covlmc() and tune_covlmc() use now nnet::multinom()
options(old_options) ## back to the previous engine
```

To use an engine only for some computations, it is simpler to rely on
`withr::with_options()` (or on `withr::local_options()` inside a
function), as done in the rest of this article.

The engine used by `covlmc()` is recorded in the model. When `prune()`
fits new models for a COVLMC (`tune_covlmc()` relies on `prune()`), it
uses the recorded engine, with a warning if the option has been changed
in between.

### A running example

We use the household electricity consumption data set
(`powerconsumption`, see also `vignette("covlmc")`), restricted to its
fifth week and discretised in three states. The covariate indicates
whether the measurement was made during the day.

```{r}
pc_week_5 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 5, ]
elec_dts <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
  labels = c("low", "typical", "high")
)
elec_cov <- data.frame(day = pc_week_5$hour >= 7 & pc_week_5$hour <= 17)
```

We select a model with the AIC with the default engine (here
`VGAM::vglm()` as the time series has three states):

```{r}
elec_glm <- tune_covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, criterion = "AIC")
elec_glm
```

and with `nnet::multinom()`:

```{r}
elec_multinom <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom"),
  tune_covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, criterion = "AIC")
)
elec_multinom
```

The two engines lead to the same context tree, with very close
likelihoods and AIC. The models are shown below with their coefficients,
first for `VGAM::vglm()`:

```{r}
model_glm <- as_covlmc(elec_glm)
draw(model_glm, model = "full")
```

and then for `nnet::multinom()`:

```{r}
model_multinom <- as_covlmc(elec_multinom)
draw(model_multinom, model = "full")
```

Most of the coefficients are identical (up to the displayed precision),
but the ones of the `high` context are very different.

### Estimation algorithms and separable data

The engines maximise the same likelihood, but with different algorithms:
`stats::glm()` and `VGAM::vglm()` use iteratively reweighted least
squares, while `nnet::multinom()` uses a quasi-Newton optimisation
method (BFGS). When the maximum likelihood estimator exists, the
algorithms reach it (up to numerical precision) and the coefficients
agree, as in most of the contexts above.

This is not the case when the data of a context are (almost) separable,
for instance when a value of a covariate determines the next state.
Let us look at the states that follow the `high` state, depending on
the value of the covariate:

```{r}
elec_states <- as.character(elec_dts)
after_high <- which(head(elec_states, -1) == "high")
high_table <- table(
  day = elec_cov$day[after_high],
  next_state = elec_states[after_high + 1]
)
high_table
```

The `high` state is never followed by the `low` one at night and very
rarely during the day (in `r high_table["TRUE", "low"]` of the
`r sum(high_table["TRUE", ])` transitions from `high`). With `low` as
the reference state, the logistic model of the `high` context describes
the logarithm of the ratio between the probability of `typical`
(respectively `high`) and the one of `low` as the sum of an intercept
and of a coefficient for `day_1TRUE`, the value of the covariate at the
time of the last `high` state. As the
probability of `low` at night is zero in the data, the maximum
likelihood intercepts are infinite (and the coefficients of `day_1TRUE`
are minus infinity, as `low` has a non-zero probability during the day).

The algorithms therefore make the intercepts grow until their stopping
criterion is met: as the likelihood barely changes once the
probability of `low` at night is small enough, the algorithms stop at
different (large) values. We can compare the probabilities estimated by
the two models of the `high` context:

```{r}
high_probs <- function(fitted) {
  coefs <- unname(as.matrix(model(find_sequence(fitted, "high"))))
  ## logits with respect to the reference state (low)
  eta <- rbind(night = c(0, coefs[, 1]), day = c(0, coefs[, 1] + coefs[, 2]))
  probs <- exp(eta) / rowSums(exp(eta))
  colnames(probs) <- states(fitted)
  probs
}
high_probs(model_glm)
high_probs(model_multinom)
```

The probabilities agree except for the probability of `low` at night,
which is tiny in both cases but differs by several orders of magnitude.
This has almost no effect on the likelihood:

```{r}
logLik(model_glm)
logLik(model_multinom)
```

In general, such differences have no practical consequences. However
the coefficients of separable contexts should not be interpreted (only
their signs are meaningful), and as `covlmc()` relies on likelihood
ratio tests to simplify the models, a test whose p-value is close to the
cut off `alpha` can lead to different decisions with the two engines,
and thus to different models.

### Convergence and the `mixvlmc.maxit` option

The maximal number of iterations of the engines is given by the
`mixvlmc.maxit` option (100 by default). When it is reached,
`stats::glm()` and `VGAM::vglm()` report a warning (a message is
reported instead when this concerns a model that is discarded because
it is rank deficient), while `nnet::multinom()` does not.

We illustrate this with a binary version of the electricity consumption
time series, for which the `"glm"` engine uses `stats::glm()`. The
following function counts the warnings emitted by an expression rather
than displaying them:

```{r}
count_warnings <- function(expr) {
  nb_warnings <- 0
  value <- withCallingHandlers(expr, warning = function(w) {
    nb_warnings <<- nb_warnings + 1
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
  list(value = value, warnings = nb_warnings)
}
elec_bin <- cut(pc_week_5$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 2, 8),
  labels = c("normal", "high")
)
bin_glm <- covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1)
bin_glm_5 <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.maxit = 5),
  count_warnings(covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1))
)
bin_glm_5$warnings
```

With at most 5 iterations, `stats::glm()` reports
`r bin_glm_5$warnings` convergence warnings, but the resulting model
has the same likelihood as the one obtained with the default number of
iterations:

```{r}
logLik(bin_glm)
logLik(bin_glm_5$value)
```

Indeed most of the warnings concern models fitted on (almost) separable
data, for which there is no finite solution to converge to: stopping
the iterations earlier has almost no effect on their likelihood. The
situation is different with `nnet::multinom()`:

```{r}
bin_multinom <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom"),
  covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1)
)
bin_multinom_5 <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom", mixvlmc.maxit = 5),
  count_warnings(covlmc(elec_bin, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1))
)
bin_multinom_5$warnings
```

No warning is reported, but the model obtained with at most 5 iterations
is not the one obtained with the default value:

```{r}
logLik(bin_multinom)
logLik(bin_multinom_5$value)
context_number(bin_multinom)
context_number(bin_multinom_5$value)
```

With three states or more, `VGAM::vglm()` also stops after
`mixvlmc.maxit` iterations and reports convergence warnings, as shown
below with the three-state time series:

```{r}
elec_vglm <- covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1)
elec_vglm_5 <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.maxit = 5),
  count_warnings(covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, alpha = 0.1))
)
elec_vglm_5$warnings
logLik(elec_vglm)
logLik(elec_vglm_5$value)
```

Here the context tree is the same (with `r context_number(elec_vglm)`
contexts), but the likelihood is slightly lower with at most 5
iterations, as some of the logistic models have not converged.

The default value of `mixvlmc.maxit` should be sufficient in most cases.
It can be increased if `stats::glm()` or `VGAM::vglm()` report
convergence warnings on contexts that are not separable. With
`nnet::multinom()`, the absence of warning does not guarantee
convergence: fitting the model again with a larger `mixvlmc.maxit` and
comparing the results is the simplest check.

### States and levels absent from a context

The data associated with a context do not necessarily contain all the
states. In the example above, the `low` state is never followed by the
`high` one, as shown by the detailed frequencies of the contexts:

```{r}
contexts(model_glm, frequency = "detailed")
```

The states that never follow a context are ignored by the model of this
context, which gives them a zero probability and has fewer coefficients:
the model of the `low` context has only one row of coefficients (it
describes the probability of `typical` relative to `low`) while the
model of the `high` context has two. This holds for all the engines.

A practical consequence is that the likelihood of new data in which
`low` is followed by `high` is zero. This is the case of the sixth week
of the data set:

```{r}
pc_week_6 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 6, ]
elec_dts_6 <- cut(pc_week_6$active_power,
  breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
  labels = c("low", "typical", "high")
)
elec_cov_6 <- data.frame(day = pc_week_6$hour >= 7 & pc_week_6$hour <= 17)
loglikelihood(model_glm, newdata = elec_dts_6, newcov = elec_cov_6)
```

Similarly, levels of factor covariates that are absent from the data of
a context are ignored by its model. The engines report this differently:
`VGAM::vglm()` gives no coefficient for those levels, while
`stats::glm()` and `nnet::multinom()` give them a zero coefficient. We
illustrate this with an artificial time series with three states whose
dynamics depend on a factor covariate `z` with three levels. The
level `w` can only be observed after state `a`:

```{r}
set.seed(2)
nb_obs <- 600
probs <- list(u = c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2), v = c(0.2, 0.6, 0.2), w = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.6))
sim_x <- character(nb_obs)
sim_z <- character(nb_obs)
sim_x[1] <- "a"
sim_z[1] <- "w"
for (t in 2:nb_obs) {
  ## the next state depends on the previous value of the covariate
  sim_x[t] <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 1, prob = probs[[sim_z[t - 1]]])
  ## w is only observed after a
  if (sim_x[t] == "a") {
    sim_z[t] <- sample(c("u", "v", "w"), 1)
  } else {
    sim_z[t] <- sample(c("u", "v"), 1)
  }
}
sim_cov <- data.frame(z = factor(sim_z))
table(sim_x, sim_z)
```

In the contexts `b` and `c`, the level `w` is absent from the data.
`VGAM::vglm()` reports no coefficient for it:

```{r}
sim_glm <- covlmc(sim_x, sim_cov)
draw(sim_glm, model = "full")
```

while `nnet::multinom()` reports a zero coefficient:

```{r}
sim_multinom <- withr::with_options(
  list(mixvlmc.predictive = "multinom"),
  covlmc(sim_x, sim_cov)
)
draw(sim_multinom, model = "full")
```

In both cases, the coefficient of `w` in the contexts `b` and `c` is
not estimated: the models are identical and so are their likelihoods.

```{r}
logLik(sim_glm)
logLik(sim_multinom)
```

The LaTeX representation produced by `draw()` (see the article
[Drawing context trees and models](drawing.html)) represents those
coefficients by zeros whatever the engine, for instance with
`VGAM::vglm()`:

```{r}
draw(sim_glm, "latex")
```

### Number of parameters

The number of parameters of a COVLMC, used by `AIC()` and `BIC()`, is
the `df` attribute of its log likelihood (see the "Number of parameters"
section of `?loglikelihood.covlmc`). As shown above, it does not depend
on the engine: the parameters that are not estimated, such as the
coefficients of the states or levels absent from the data of a context,
are not counted, regardless of the way the engine reports them.

More precisely, the model of a context followed by $k$ different states
in the data has $(k-1)q$ parameters, where $q$ is the number of
parameters associated with the covariates: one for the intercept and,
for each time step of the memory of the model, one per numerical or
logical covariate and the number of levels minus one per factor
covariate (counting only the levels present in the data of the
context). The following code recomputes the number of parameters of each
context of the electricity consumption example from its detailed
frequencies and from the memory of its model:

```{r}
elec_ctx <- contexts(model_glm, frequency = "detailed", hsize = TRUE)
nb_states <- rowSums(elec_ctx[, as.character(states(model_glm))] > 0)
q <- 1 + elec_ctx$hsize
elec_ctx$parameters <- (nb_states - 1) * q
elec_ctx$nominal <- (length(states(model_glm)) - 1) * q
elec_ctx[, c("context", "hsize", "parameters", "nominal")]
sum(elec_ctx$parameters)
attr(logLik(model_glm), "df")
```

For instance, the `low` context (first row) is followed by
$k = `r nb_states[1]`$ different states and its model has a memory of
`r elec_ctx$hsize[1]` time step of the logical covariate, thus
$q = `r q[1]`$ and `r elec_ctx$parameters[1]` parameters.

The likelihood ratio tests used by `covlmc()` to simplify the models
use instead the *nominal* number of parameters, $(s-1)q$, where $s$ is
the number of states and $q$ counts all the levels of the factor
covariates, as in the original algorithm. In this example, the sum of
the nominal numbers of parameters of the contexts would be
`r sum(elec_ctx$nominal)` instead of `r attr(logLik(model_glm), "df")`.

## Degenerate contexts

When a context is always followed by the same state in the data, the
maximum likelihood estimate of the probability of this state is one,
and the logistic models are degenerate. `covlmc()` does not call the
engine in this case but uses a *constant model* that does not depend on
the covariates. Its probabilities are regularised: they are computed
after adding `pseudo_obs` fake observations of each of the states to
the observed ones. If the context is followed $n$ times by the state
$x$ and the state space contains $s$ states, the probability of $x$ is
$$
\frac{n+\text{pseudo\_obs}}{n+s\times\text{pseudo\_obs}},
$$
while the other states have a probability of
$\frac{\text{pseudo\_obs}}{n+s\times\text{pseudo\_obs}}$. This
corresponds to a Bayesian posterior mean estimation with a Dirichlet
prior. The `pseudo_obs` parameter is set with `covlmc_control()` and
defaults to 1.

We illustrate this with an artificial binary time series in which state
1 is always followed by state 0, while the probability of switching from
0 to 1 increases with a numerical covariate:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
nb_obs <- 500
deg_cov <- data.frame(y = runif(nb_obs))
deg_x <- integer(nb_obs)
for (t in 2:nb_obs) {
  if (deg_x[t - 1] == 1) {
    deg_x[t] <- 0L
  } else {
    deg_x[t] <- rbinom(1, 1, 0.2 + 0.6 * deg_cov$y[t - 1])
  }
}
deg_model <- covlmc(deg_x, deg_cov)
draw(deg_model, model = "full")
```

The context 1 has a constant model, with only an intercept. As the time
series has two states, this intercept is the logit of the probability of
state 1. In the data, the context is followed
`r contexts(deg_model, frequency = "detailed")[["0"]][2]` times by state
0:

```{r}
deg_ctx <- contexts(deg_model, frequency = "detailed", model = "coef")
deg_ctx
```

and the probability of state 1 after state 1 is therefore
`1 / (n + 2)` (with `pseudo_obs = 1`):

```{r}
n_1 <- deg_ctx[["0"]][2]
plogis(deg_ctx$coef[[2]][1])
1 / (n_1 + 2)
```

The `pseudo_obs` parameter can be given to `covlmc()` (and to
`tune_covlmc()`) via a `control` list created by `covlmc_control()`.
`covlmc()` also accepts it directly as an argument, which is passed to
`covlmc_control()`. Larger values lead to less extreme probabilities:

```{r}
pseudo_obs_values <- c(0.1, 1, 10)
deg_models <- lapply(pseudo_obs_values, function(po) {
  covlmc(deg_x, deg_cov, control = covlmc_control(pseudo_obs = po))
})
data.frame(
  pseudo_obs = pseudo_obs_values,
  prob_1_after_1 = sapply(deg_models, function(m) {
    plogis(contexts(m, model = "coef")$coef[[2]][1])
  }),
  expected = pseudo_obs_values / (n_1 + 2 * pseudo_obs_values),
  loglikelihood = sapply(deg_models, function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m)))
)
```

The regularised probabilities are used to compute the likelihood, which
decreases when `pseudo_obs` increases as the probability of the observed
transition decreases. The model of a context followed by a single state
has no parameter (see the previous section), so `pseudo_obs` has no
effect on the number of parameters:

```{r}
attr(logLik(deg_models[[1]]), "df")
attr(logLik(deg_models[[3]]), "df")
```

Notice that the regularisation applies only to contexts followed by a
single state: in the other contexts, states that never follow the
context have a zero probability, as explained above.

## Memory occupation and trimming

### What a COVLMC stores

A `covlmc` object contains the fitted engine objects (one per context,
plus the ones used to compute the likelihood of the first observations,
see `vignette("likelihood")`) as well as the data used to fit them. When
`keep_data = TRUE` (the default value), `covlmc()` also stores the
original time series and covariates, and caches some models, in order
to enable post-pruning with `prune()` (and thus `tune_covlmc()`). The
engine objects themselves store quantities whose size grows with the
number of observations (such as fitted values and residuals) and their
formulas reference the environment in which they were created.

As a consequence, COVLMC objects can be large. Two measures of size are
given below: `object.size()` ignores environments, while the size of the
serialised object includes them and corresponds to what is written by
`saveRDS()` (without compression) or sent to the workers in parallel
processing. Neither is exactly the memory used by the object in the R
session.

```{r}
obj_sizes <- function(...) {
  objects <- list(...)
  data.frame(
    object_size_kb = sapply(objects, function(o) {
      round(as.numeric(object.size(o)) / 1024)
    }),
    serialised_kb = sapply(objects, function(o) {
      round(length(serialize(o, NULL)) / 1024)
    })
  )
}
obj_sizes(
  "VGAM::vglm()" = model_glm,
  "nnet::multinom()" = model_multinom
)
```

The two measures do not agree, as they do not account for the
components of the objects in the same way, but both show that the
models fitted by `VGAM::vglm()` are much larger than the ones fitted by
`nnet::multinom()`.

### Trimming a model

The `trim()` function (see `trim.covlmc()`) removes the data and the
cached models from a COVLMC. With `keep_model = TRUE`, the engine
objects are kept but simplified (with `butcher::butcher()` for
`stats::glm()` and `nnet::multinom()`) and the environments referenced
by their formulas are discarded. With `keep_model = FALSE` (default),
the engine objects are removed and only their coefficients are kept.

```{r}
obj_sizes(
  "untrimmed" = model_glm,
  "trim(keep_model = TRUE)" = trim(model_glm, keep_model = TRUE),
  "trim()" = trim(model_glm)
)
```

The fully trimmed model is very small, but it supports fewer
operations. The following table summarises what can be done with a
model trimmed with `keep_model = TRUE` or `keep_model = FALSE` (see the
documentation of the corresponding functions):

| Operation                                   | `TRUE` | `FALSE` |
|:--------------------------------------------|:------:|:-------:|
| `logLik()`, `AIC()`, `BIC()`                | yes    | yes     |
| `draw()`, `contexts(model = "coef")`        | yes    | yes     |
| `contexts(metrics = TRUE)`                  | yes    | yes     |
| `contexts(model = "full")`                  | yes    | no      |
| `model(type = "full")`                      | yes    | no      |
| `loglikelihood()` on new data               | yes    | no      |
| `predict()`, `simulate()`                   | yes    | no      |
| `metrics()` of the model                    | no     | no      |
| `positions()`, `contexts(positions = TRUE)` | no     | no      |
| `prune()`                                   | no     | no      |

For instance, the likelihood of the original data is preserved by
trimming, while the likelihood of new data needs the engine objects:

```{r, error = TRUE}
elec_trimmed <- trim(model_glm)
logLik(elec_trimmed)
loglikelihood(trim(model_glm, keep_model = TRUE),
  newdata = elec_dts_6, newcov = elec_cov_6
)
loglikelihood(elec_trimmed, newdata = elec_dts_6, newcov = elec_cov_6)
```

As `prune()` is not available for trimmed models, the trimming should be
done once the model selection is completed.

### Trimming in `tune_covlmc()`

`tune_covlmc()` builds a sequence of models by pruning an initial large
model and can save some of them. The `trimming` argument specifies the
trimming of the intermediate models (`"full"` by default, which
corresponds to `trim()`, `"partial"`, which corresponds to
`trim(keep_model = TRUE)`, or `"none"`), while `best_trimming` applies
to the best model and to the initial one, which are not trimmed by
default (see `vignette("model-selection")` and the "Memory occupation"
section of `?tune_covlmc`). Trimming all the models, including the best
one, is recommended when memory is an issue, in particular when
`tune_covlmc()` is called in parallel processing contexts:

```{r}
elec_glm_trimmed <- tune_covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov,
  criterion = "AIC",
  best_trimming = "full"
)
obj_sizes(
  "default" = elec_glm,
  "best_trimming = \"full\"" = elec_glm_trimmed
)
```

The trimmed result still gives access to the selected model and to the
results of the selection process, for instance:

```{r}
elec_glm_trimmed
```
